procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 13.01.2016 of the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Criminal Appeal No. 1390 of 2006.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad reversed the acquittal ordered by the trial court and convicted the appellant under Section 376(2)(f) IPC, sentencing him to ten years rigorous imprisonment, with fine of Rs.5,000/- along with a default stipulation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant assails his conviction by the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Sufficiency of evidence for identification of the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The Test Identification Parade (T.I.P.) is only corroborative evidence and cannot be treated as substantive evidence for conviction.
There is no other evidence to prove the appellant's identity as the perpetrator.
Dock identification of the appellant was declined.
respondent_arguments: The available evidence unequivocally establishes the appellant as the perpetrator of the sexual assault.

arguments.issue_text: Admissibility and procedural handling of the serological report.
appellant_arguments: The serological report was not formally exhibited, and its author was not examined.
No questions regarding the serological report were put to the appellant under Section 313 Cr.P.C., denying him an opportunity for defense.
Due to these procedural lapses, the conviction is unsustainable.
respondent_arguments: The serologist report is an expert opinion under Section 45 of the Evidence Act, 1872.
It is admissible in evidence without being formally marked as an exhibit or being proved by oral evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: It would be a travesty of justice to acquit the appellant merely because the prosecutrix turned hostile and failed to identify him in the dock, especially in view of the other overwhelming evidence available, such as medical evidence confirming the sexual assault.
legal_tests_applied: A balancing test where the presumption of innocence for the accused must be weighed against the rights of the victim and the societal interest in the preservation of the rule of law.
why_appellant_lost: The court refused to acquit based on the prosecutrix turning hostile and failing to make a dock identification, finding that there was other overwhelming evidence, including medical evidence that confirmed the sexual assault and a non-doubtful Test Identification Parade (T.I.P.).

The failure of the trial court to put questions about the serological report to the appellant under Section 313 Cr.P.C. was deemed a procedural lapse by the court, for which the victim should not suffer; it was not considered a fatal flaw justifying acquittal.
why_respondent_won: The conviction was upheld because the court found that other corroborative evidence, such as the medical report, was sufficient to prove the crime, thereby overcoming the failure of the prosecutrix to identify the appellant in court.

The court held that a procedural omission by the trial court, such as the failure to question the accused on a piece of evidence under Section 313 Cr.P.C., does not automatically vitiate the trial or warrant an acquittal.
policy_considerations: A criminal trial is a quest for truth, and the dispensation of justice cannot be allowed to become a mockery by simply allowing prime prosecution witnesses to turn hostile as a ground for acquittal.
Neither the accused nor the victim should be permitted to subvert a criminal trial by stating falsehoods and resorting to contrivances.
Criminal justice is not one-sided and must draw a balance between conflicting rights and duties; the victim should not suffer for the laches or omissions of the court.
